summary: This issue of South Korean Interim Government Activities (No. 32, prepared by the National Economic Board) covers May 1948, a month dominated by the 10 May general election, the first in Korean history, with about 91 percent of registrants voting despite communist terror. Nearly half of the 198 elected Assemblymen were rightists, Rhee Syngman became Assembly chairman, and the Assembly convened on 31 May. North Korea's 14 May electricity cutoff discredited Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic after the Pyongyang conference and cut industrial output about 75 percent, while drought threatened summer grain. The report also covers the Cheju rebellion, border incidents, sabotage, Mukden repatriates, vested property Koreanization, court reorganization, education ordinances and women's participation. Detailed tables on prices, coal, trade, petroleum, transport, power, finance and insurance give historians a month-by-month statistical baseline for the last weeks of the Interim Government.
highlights: 10 May 1948: first free general election; more than 91 percent of registrants voted despite communist violence.
North Korea cut electricity to the South on 14 May, ending roughly 60 percent of supply.
Overall industrial production fell about 75 percent by end of May due to power shortage.
Elections in two of three Cheju districts were invalid; virtual civil war continued on the island.
Ordinance No. 192 separated Korean courts from the Department of Justice.
Three education ordinances drafted to create school districts and Boards of Education.
First Mukden repatriates (3,800 in four ships) arrived at Inchon.
Thirty-one 38th parallel border incidents with North Korean Constabulary reported.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 32 (May 1948), prepared by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK, followed by blank and image pages. Lists Board members at 31 May 1948, including Chairman Wilhelm Anderson, Executive Secretary Otis T. Weaver and directors for Agriculture, Commerce, Finance and Transportation, plus a six-part table of contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Reviews May 1948 as historic: the 10 May election drew 91 per cent of registrants despite communist terror, and the Assembly sat 31 May. North Korea's 14 May power cutoff cut production about 75 per cent and discredited Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic. Also covers drought, Cheju rebellion, border incidents, rising trade, 469,000,000 won note issue and rice prices.

sections.title: Part I. Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population, repatriation and foreign affairs, plus vested property administration.

sections.title: Section 1. Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: South Korea's population rose one-third since 1940, reaching about 20,041,000 by January 1948; net migration added roughly 1,534,000. Refugees from the north fell about 20 per cent from April; the first Mukden repatriates reached Inchon on 11 May (3,831 by month end). Covers Korean schooling disputes in Japan, repatriating businessmen, and a new immigration ordinance expected about 1 August.

sections.title: Section 2. Vested Property
sections.summary: The Office of Property Custody prepared for Koreanization by decentralizing operations and training auditors. A record 2,334 financial statements arrived, and the Korean Residence Management Corporation was taken over on 6 May. Purchase applications rose after the election (497 cases), sales totaled 111,225 thousand won, and rent collections and loan guarantees continued; Allied nationals' property was reviewed.

sections.title: Part II. Production and Supply
sections.summary: Agriculture, prices, industry, mining, allocation, trade and labor.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Summer grain forecast of 673,982 metric tons on 1,956,227 acres (104.1 per cent of 1947) faced reduced yields from drought, and 94,153 acres of rice land depended on power pumps. Reports covered livestock, fertilizer, forestry tables, fisheries exports to Japan worth $4,936,162, KAA fertilizer sales, 448,513 farms sold by the National Land Administration, and the Agricultural Improvement Service.

sections.title: Section 2. Prices
sections.summary: Open-market wholesale prices in Seoul rose in May: rice up nearly 10 per cent to about the January level, with barley, red beans, building materials, metals and raw silk higher. Retail prices increased after a March-April dip, while sugar, salt, dried fish, laundry soap and work shoes fell. Nine-city rice averaged 734 won by 25 May; National Price Administration controlled prices are tabulated.

sections.title: Section 3. Industrial Production
sections.summary: Power cutoff from North Korea on 14 May cut overall production about 75 per cent by month end, reversing a strong April (rubber shoes from 154 plants, 2,261,906 pairs; cigarettes up 66.2 per cent). May hit flour, paper (166.9 tons), cement, bricks, briquettes and cotton goods, while salt rose to 28,056 tons. Production statistics cover under 100 larger plants.

sections.title: Section 4. Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output reached 68,612 metric tons in April, up 9.3 per cent and more than double the 1947 average, with Samchuk exceeding quota; the May power cutoff then reduced mining, flooded the Ongjin and Haeju mines, and Yong Wol fell to 6,639 tons. Bituminous imports from Japan dropped to 61,068 tons from 83,171. The Coal Industry Fund sought a 200,000,000 won loan.

sections.title: Section 5. Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: The Consumer Goods Allocation Board dealt with delayed cotton cloth deliveries over price differences. Civilian supply allocations went to Commerce, Agriculture and other departments; May petroleum allocations included 6,936,921 liters of gasoline for elections. Salt distribution reached 27,434 tons, ex-Japanese metals were allocated, and Federation of Financial Associations goods reached employees.

sections.title: Section 6. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: May licenses (95 import, 83 export) pointed to exports near 548 million won against imports near 323 million. April private trade: imports 746 million won (paper products, rubber, drugs), exports 391 million (dried fish over half), 99 percent to Hong Kong, 87 percent of imports via Inchon. Government sales of ore and graphite, Civilian Supply coal, fertilizer, flour, sugar and petroleum are also covered.

sections.title: Section 7. Labor
sections.summary: Strike threats hit two industries in May. At Seoul Electric the Tai Han union denied a communist-inspired strike, the Military Governor approved Maj.-Gen. Dean's fact-finding report, and a 29 May conference followed. At Pusan, after wildcat stoppages of 450 stevedores on 11-12 May, contractors fell to seven or eight, a joint hiring hall replaced the honcho system, and the union deferred strikes. Child labor and overtime inspections, a renamed labor paper, and radio and health items also appear.

sections.title: Part III. Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, utilities and public works.

sections.title: Section 1. Transportation
sections.summary: Communist sabotage around the 10 May election wrecked train No. 36, pulled rails and spikes, and damaged locomotives at several cities. Marine shipping priorities were readjusted, coal first at 42.9 percent. April Transportation revenue fell 28 percent to 374.6 million won. Rail employment rose 2.3 percent, 17 more locomotives became operable, and coal moved from Mukko. Refugees were repatriated from Tientsin.

sections.title: Section 2. Communications
sections.summary: Saboteurs burned the Inchon telephone exchange (repairs of two to three months, about 7 million won) and arsonists destroyed the Yongdungpo repeater station on 23 May, killing two employees and a policeman. April revenue fell 30.6 percent from March, staff declined to 12,761, and postal deposits, book transfers and life insurance are tabulated. Phone and telegraph rates, about 85 times 1937 levels, rose at the end of May.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Utilities
sections.summary: May power distribution fell to 56.1 million KWH from 74.5 million in April; South Korea produced 41.5 million and the North delivered 15.1 million before the 14 May shut-off. The Emergency Power Board set Daylight Saving Time from 31 May, 30-watt home bulbs and new priorities, and US monitoring of dispatch began 26 May. Sun Jin Gang hit a record output; Seoul streetcars resumed within 45 minutes.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Works
sections.summary: A stocktaking of two and a half years credited Public Works with rebuilding the Seoul-Pusan Highway (37 bridges, 497 km, about 236.8 million won), 162 km of levees, water plants, fire service reorganization and 515 pieces of heavy equipment. May brought a road competition won by Cholla-namdo, bridge progress, 153 million won in flood subsidies, power-cut water problems, and 181 fires.

sections.title: Part IV. Finance
sections.summary: Government and non-government finance.

sections.title: Section 1. Government Finance
sections.summary: The Bank of Chosun note issue peaked at 33,389 million won in December 1947 and was down 4,745 million by May, though May rose 469 million. The overdraft stood at 20,232 million won after a 4,424 million credit. F/Y 1947/48 authorizations reached 22,320 million; F/Y 1948/49 budgets approximate 29 billion. April revenue was 1,930 million (tobacco 702 million), expenditure 2,010 million, revenue-to-spending ratio 73 percent; Civilian Supply assets 22,995 million.

sections.title: Section 2. Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: April data only. Cash balances fell 1,080 million won to 2,428.7 million, and deposits reached a record 56,421 million (55 percent government). Loans outstanding fell 2,096 million to 30,025 million, the fourth monthly net retirement. Life insurance in force rose 68 million won; damage insurers wrote 8,294 policies. May loans approved totaled 1,839 million, and banks were told to compile claims against Japan.

sections.title: Part V. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, politics, legal affairs, police and interzone matters.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: Chief Adviser Dr. Edgar Johnson returned on 25 May from Washington after 72 conferences on budgets, supplies, Japan trade and post-transfer planning. The National Economic Board met four times on budgets, rates and grain prices. Provincial civil service officers met in Seoul; pay rises of 25 to 130 percent were approved from 1 June, tied to staff cuts. Military Government personnel were 3,003 in May.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Developments
sections.summary: 10 May general election (91% turnout, 198 seats), National Assembly opening, Pyongyang North-South conference outcome, power shut-off effects on Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic, Koreans in Japan.

sections.title: General Election
sections.summary: On 10 May over 91 percent of registrants voted in Korea's first general election with little sabotage. Of 198 members, nearly half were rightists, none communist, and Hankook Democratic Party was strongest; two Cheju districts were voided. Party and occupation tables, rightist praise, moderate and Kim Koo objections that the vote was unfree, and an average age of 47 are included.

sections.title: National Assembly
sections.summary: Rhee Syngman said after the election that the Assembly's decisions would be state law and preferred the American presidential system. A preliminary meeting on 27 May saw 149 members elect him temporary chairman. On 31 May all 198 attended, Rhee won the speakership with 188 votes, Shin Ik-hi and Kim Tong-won became vice-speakers, and Hodge and Dean spoke at the opening.

sections.title: North-South Conference
sections.summary: Kimm Kiu-sic and Kim Koo returned from Pyongyang on 5 May after the 19-25 April conference. They reported a four-Kim agreement to oppose a separate southern government, demand withdrawal of US and Soviet forces, and hold a later North-South conference. Their 5 May statement said the North promised no separate government; the text breaks off in the electricity assurance.

sections.title: Power Shut-off
sections.summary: North Korea cut off electricity to the South on 14 May, citing unpaid bills and the refusal of USAFIK, which does not recognize the North Korean People's Committee, to send a delegation. Rightists blamed the Soviets and communists blamed the United States. Kim Koo disclaimed knowledge of the contract, and some saw benefit in forcing self-sufficiency.

sections.title: Koreans in Japan
sections.summary: Several South Korean parties had for months protested treatment of Koreans in Japan, calling it a revival of Japanese imperialism. Reports that a number of Korean schools in Japan had been closed were read as an infringement of Korean rights. Protests came from all political factions, as already noted in the April report.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Ordinance No. 192 reorganized the courts, separating them from the Department of Justice from 1 June, alongside Ordinances 193-197, two USAFIK proclamations (daylight-saving time, National Assembly's first meeting). Opinions covered vested property and silk profiteering. Prison population was 22,141; Cheju trials were expedited; the Civil Code gained an air-carriers section; 49 vested-property claims were screened administratively.

sections.title: Section 4. National Police
sections.summary: Violence around the 10 May election killed four candidates, 15 election officials and 32 policemen, with about 275 civilian deaths; only 68 of 13,407 booths were attacked. Fighting on Cheju-do intensified, with 3,126 held and two districts unable to vote. The section also describes police financing through contributions and the effective Pusan police under Chief Pak.

sections.title: Section 5. Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Thirty-one border incidents with North Korean Constabulary occurred, mostly near the Oe-dong dam, and an American civilian was wounded on 26 May. A Soviet Yak-9 landed near Yosu. About 43,000 pieces of mail were exchanged, down from 59,000 in April. Radio Pyongyang attacked the election, the Americans and the power issue.

sections.title: Part VI. Social
sections.summary: Health, education, culture, press opinion, youth and women.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Repatriation of Mukden refugees began, with four ships carrying about 3,800 people through Inchon quarantine camps and a low disease rate; smallpox appeared on Cheju. Kyongsang-namdo completed 2,106 low-cost housing units, UNRRA grants aided orphanages and training schools, and nursing, veterinary, pharmaceutical, narcotics and laboratory matters were reported.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: Three ordinances were drafted creating school districts, Boards of Education and a household-income-tax basis for school finance, replacing land-value taxes eroded by inflation. The FY 1948/49 budget was 1.5 billion won. Unified teacher certification starts 15 June; 845 teachers will attend summer sessions. Bureau reports covered textbooks (13.9 million printed), tests, language institute and vocational education.

sections.title: Section 3. Culture
sections.summary: Thirty-organization election campaign teams gave 803 performances to 1,334,464 people from 7 April. Music news covered the first Musical Festival, Beethoven concerts and scholarships for three Korean musicians. The Seoul U.S. Information Center opened 29 April; art exhibits, Children's Day, election stamps issued 10 May, and KBS election coverage were also reported.

sections.title: Section 4. Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The press debated the Pyongyang Conference and the broken power promise, then covered the 10 May election. A police report listed 202 dead and 643 wounded from 31 March to 17 May; moderate and rightist papers praised the election, while the Country Guard Corps was ordered disbanded on 22 May. Rhee's press conference, power cutoff and fear of Japan also drew comment.

sections.title: Section 5. Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Thirty-three KNY members were elected to the National Assembly, mostly as rightist-backed candidates or independents, far outnumbering Dai Dong's 13. Audited membership reached 859,208 (605,316 men, 109,899 women, 93,910 maritime, 50,083 students), with a fifth screening ordered. The FY 1948/49 allocation was 20,600,000 won; May projects included literacy classes and road repair.

sections.title: Section 6. Women's Activities
sections.summary: About 3,000,000 women voted on 10 May, roughly half of 7,908,892 registered voters (3,903,293 women); 19 of 594 candidates were women and none was elected. The Women's Bureau ran a Mothers' School, and the Korean women's federation was admitted to the American federation. Volunteer service, Junior Red Cross gift boxes, a YWCA fashion show and Ewha University's curriculum followed.

sections.title: Back matter
sections.summary: Back matter consists of blank pages, a library date-due slip (stamped June 2010) with a barcode number, and a closing source note giving the UCSF Industry Documents Library URL. It contains no report content.
